Sources: new-york/AUTHORITY-MAP-NEW-YORK.md + new-york/SPEED-RULES-NEW-YORK.md + new-york/hub.json (geometry, gates) + PUBLIC-PARTNERS-BRIEF.md patterns. CONTRACT v3: only `title` (≤6 words), `value`/figures, `note` (≤140 chars, partner-clean plain English), `status` (enum: market_priced | modeled | upside), and `fn` (footnote key) render — plus verbatim copy fields (headline/subline/lead/body/chips/cards). Underscore-prefixed fields NEVER reach the DOM. null/missing = render nothing. Footnotes render ONCE in a single 'Notes & assumptions' section above the contact form; a footnote's source_url may render as a small domain chip, never as a naked URL in body copy. Never render: held corridors, Gulf counterparties, authority contacts, internal dock-status fields. NY NOTES: posture is DUAL (Operate-weighted in NYC proper via NYCEDC/NYC DOT; Enable across the NJ/Westchester/LI/CT ring) — data.weighting = balanced with framing copy carrying the split. Speed-rule section is deliberately narrow: NY's binding rules are near-dock bands; the historic East River 10-kn rule was superseded in 2024 and the page makes no claim either way about East River speed law. Bodies with unverified posture (Weehawken, West New York, CT DOT, East End villages) are omitted. hub.json gates honored: forbid_employer_names, banned term 'Williamsburg', ny_c_honesty (no raw-speed claims vs Metro-North).

copy.lead: New York is already asking this question. The city's own Comprehensive Waterfront Plan calls for "an equitable, resilient and healthy waterfront for all New Yorkers" — and the city already owns and runs the largest public commuter-ferry system in the country.
copy.support: Since 2025, every car trip into the Manhattan core pays a $9 congestion toll. The city's own policy prices the road; the water is the relief it left open.

copy.framing: Two ways to partner — a genuine choice. New York is both at once: the strongest public-operator water-transit market in the country inside the city, and a ring of ready municipal landings around it.
copy.enable_track: Grant landing access at existing public landings, piers, and marinas, and a permitting pathway for a pilot corridor. Private capital finances the fleet; privately committed demand fills the seats. The ask is access, not money.
copy.operate_track: New York's public bodies already own and operate ferry fleets at national scale. Navier vessels can be procured the way transit vehicles are procured — to augment the public water network, or to add a premium tier on corridors it doesn't serve.

operate_proof_points.proof: Owns the 38-vessel NYC Ferry system, run day to day by a contracted private operator — the largest public-ferry precedent in the country, and structurally the exact frame the Operate track proposes.
Operates the free, 24/7 Staten Island Ferry directly — public vessel operation at scale, in-house.

copy.headline: Your speed rules were written for boats that make wake.
copy.framing: New York's binding water rules sit at the dock, not on the open water: 5 mph within 100 feet of any New York shore or dock, slow-no-wake within 200 feet of any New Jersey marina or pier, and per-harbor zones in Connecticut. Open water runs on the federal safe-speed duty — a judgment standard these rules exist to serve: controlling wake, wash, noise, and disturbance. A foiling, electric Navier satisfies those outcomes inherently.
copy.ask: Our ask is modest here, and mostly Connecticut-shaped: measure us. Where independent wake and noise measurement shows a rule's purpose is served, grant route-specific relief through the mechanisms your own rules already provide.

expander.title: What speed-rule relief unlocks
body: In New York, honestly: not much on most corridors. The near-dock slow zones are short, and every schedule respects them anyway — we do not ask for relief there.

The exception is Connecticut. In harbors with long no-wake channels, measured-wake relief could recover a few minutes per call — worth pursuing corridor by corridor, only after each harbor's own rules are confirmed.

One point of historical honesty: an older East River speed rule was superseded in 2024 by an unrelated provision. We make no claim either way about East River speed law — this page simply publishes schedule times that respect posted and local limits everywhere.
Precedent: Stockholm's public transport authority runs an electric hydrofoil ferry at roughly twice the posted zone speed under a low-wake exemption.

rule_basis.detail: 5 mph within 100 ft of shore, dock, pier, raft, float, or anchored/moored vessel
slow speed / no wake within 200 ft of any marina, pier, dock, wharf, or abutment — explicitly wake-framed; cleanest fit for the foiling low-wake argument
state-appointed harbormasters set speed/no-wake zones in Stamford, Norwalk, Bridgeport etc.; per-harbor ordinances not primary-verified this pass — verify before publishing CT segment times
open-water conduct is safe-speed judgment; N45 (20 pax) falls below VTS NY participation thresholds; episodic COTP zones only

rule_basis.instrument: Former East River RNA (33 CFR § 165.166, 2002 ed.)
rule_basis.detail: no-wake / ≤10 kn East River rule — SUPERSEDED: the section number now holds a 2024 drone-display safety-zone rule. Per SPEED-RULES-NEW-YORK.md §4: never claim the East River is speed-capped, never claim it is affirmatively uncapped; verify with USCG Sector New York before any in-page claim

navier_intro.title: Meet the vessel

copy.headline: Zero-emission. Near-silent. Almost no wake.
copy.subline: Navier is a U.S. builder of electric hydrofoil vessels — the traits that matter for harbor rules and harbor neighbors are built into the hull, not bolted on.
copy.body: The N45 Explorer carries 20 passengers at a foilborne cruise speed of about 20 knots, lifted clear of the water for a smooth, wake-free ride. The smaller N30 Quanta carries 8. Foiling cuts energy use by up to ~90% versus a conventional planing hull, and both vessels run near-silent on electric power.

tech_chips.value: up to ~90% less than a planing hull

reference.title: Reference

copy.intro: New York Harbor's water-transportation landscape spans city, bi-state, state, and municipal bodies across four states' worth of shoreline. We seek conversations — nothing here implies approval, endorsement, or commitment by any body named.

bodies.role: Owns the 38-vessel NYC Ferry system, run by a contracted private operator; also operates the Atlantic Basin landing and the Blue Highways waterborne-freight program.
Operates the Staten Island Ferry and owns the public ferry landings at Pier 11/Wall St, East 34th Street, and Pier 79 — the Manhattan ends of every line on this network.
Authors the Comprehensive Waterfront Plan — the city's 10-year waterfront vision and its waterborne-transportation strategies.
State-city partnership controlling the Hudson-bank park piers from the Battery to W 59th; landing only at designated locations, confirmed parcel by parcel.

bodies.body: Port Authority of New York & New Jersey
bodies.role: Bi-state port district; underlying owner at Atlantic Basin (transfer to the city announced 2024) and co-funder of the Hoboken ferry-slip restoration.
Owns Hoboken Terminal, whose historic ferry slips were restored (~$125M with the Port Authority) expressly to allow expansion of ferry service.

bodies.body: Brooklyn Bridge Park Corp · Brooklyn Navy Yard Development Corp · Roosevelt Island Operating Corp
bodies.role: Park, campus, and island corporations controlling the BBP Pier 6, Dock 72, and Roosevelt Island landings.
Owns a federally funded ferry terminal at Garvies Point, built in 2015 and still without regular service — a ready landing seeking a network.

bodies.body: Harbor cities and towns — Edgewater, Yonkers, New Rochelle, North Hempstead (Port Washington), Greenwich, Milford
bodies.role: Own their municipal landings; none operates commuter vessels. Yonkers' pier is being rebuilt; Greenwich already runs seasonal town ferries.
State-appointed harbormasters govern vessel speed and harbor use in Stamford, Norwalk, and Bridgeport; several Connecticut landings are private marinas reached by commercial agreement.

bodies.body: US Coast Guard Sector New York · US Army Corps of Engineers
bodies.role: Navigation and channel stewardship — vessel traffic service, federal channels, episodic safety zones. Permitting context, not landing grantors.
